chapter: Bix's methods and New Orleans musicians
title: How Bix composed and Chink Martin's Bix story
summary: Bix told Hug he worked at the piano; Chink Martin recalled Bix sitting in with the Rhythm Kings.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, what I asked him mostly about was, was, was, was how did he go about, how did he go about giving away these souls out? And like you say, he told me that most of the times he would be sitting down, reminiscing a little bit by himself. He said he liked to work alone. And I can understand that, you know. He said he'd be by himself and he'd sit down and he'd be playing a few chords. And first thing you know, he'd get an inspiration for something, you know. And he'd jot it down because, you know, they say he didn't read. He didn't know how to read, but he couldn't read, you know. He could. Oh, yeah. He could read. And he told me that he did study, you know. But he didn't, he didn't study extensively, you know. Yeah. But he did, he did know, he did know something about music. And he, he, he, he could work out a lot of these things. And I imagine that he, he probably, like, I didn't ask him what was his favorite classical music composers or anything like that. But I imagine that he did have them. And, and he did, he did, he told me that he worked, like you asked me about before, that I think that he worked these things out on piano. He said that he did sit down and work a lot of these things out on piano.

Yeah. Oh. Of course, it was very simple for him to take it and put it on the cornet once he, once he, once he, he worked it out on piano. Mm. You see, because he, his harmonies, he relied on his harmonies so much. That's what he told me. His changes, his chord progressions. Mm-hmm. It brings to mind right there a very funny story about Chink Morton, the old bass player. Mm-hmm. Who is 88 years old today. He played, he played with, with the Red Dead Kings for a while.
And he told me when they were at Fry's Inn in Chicago that Bix used to come around there.

Well, that was about 1921, 22. I guess Bix, Bix was quite young then. And he, it shows how much he liked the New Orleans musicians. He'd come around them and he used to want to sit in and he'd play in between when they'd be off the stand, he'd be on the piano, you know, playing around with the piano. He'd be on the piano, playing all these funny chords and everything. And then he wanted to sit in and play with them. So, with those chords that he was playing, these fellas, they couldn't, they couldn't, they didn't know what he was doing, you know. Because he was playing all of these augmented sevens and augmented nines and sided fifths and a lot of, a lot of chords that were far beyond what they were using, you know. These late teats and things like that. So, he said that Paul Perez told him. Now, Paul Perez later on, in later years now, got to, got to really respect him and admire him, you know. But this was in the early part I'm talking about. Paul didn't understand it either. And Paul told Jake Martin, he says, say what you do, he says, don't let that, whatever you do, don't let that guy get on the piano. And he says, he says, because he runs me crazy. He couldn't understand what he was doing, you know.
